title: Food Preservation
summary: How to store and preserve meat, fish, and plants without electricity.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Dehydrate and Air-Dry
sections.body: Dehydration removes moisture, preventing mold and bacterial growth. Slice meat (for jerky) or fruits very thinly (under 1/4 inch). Hang the slices on racks or lines in a hot, dry, breezy location. Cover with mesh or cheesecloth to keep flies and insects away.
sections.warning: Do not dry meat in humid or rainy conditions, as it will spoil before it dehydrates.
sections.image_description: Thin strips of meat hanging on string under the sun

sections.heading: Step 2 — Smoke Cure Meat and Fish
sections.body: Smoking preserves food through drying and the antibacterial properties of wood smoke. Build a simple A-frame smokehouse or use an enclosed barrel. Burn hardwood (like oak, hickory, or apple) to create cool, steady smoke. Hang meat/fish inside for 24 to 48 hours.
sections.warning: Never use pine, fir, or other resinous softwoods, as their smoke contains toxic resins.
sections.image_description: Fish hanging inside a wooden smokehouse with smoke rising from below

sections.heading: Step 3 — Salt and Pickle
sections.body: Salting draws moisture out of meat and inhibits bacterial growth. Pack meat slices tightly in clean jars or crocks, layering them heavily with coarse, non-iodized salt. For vegetables, submerge them in a clean brine of water, salt, and vinegar (if available) to ferment and preserve.
sections.warning: Always rinse heavily salted meat thoroughly in clean water before cooking and consuming.
sections.image_description: Glass jar showing layers of white salt and red meat

sections.heading: Step 4 — Build a Root Cellar or Cache
sections.body: Keep root vegetables (potatoes, carrots, onions) in a cool, dark, and damp space to prevent sprouting and rotting. Dig a pit or trench in well-drained soil, line it with straw, place the vegetables inside, cover with more straw, and top with dirt to insulate against freezing.
sections.warning: Do not store bruised or damaged crops, as they will rot and spoil the rest of the batch.
sections.image_description: Cross-section diagram of an underground root cellar lined with straw

when_to_use: When you have a surplus of food (such as after a successful hunt or harvest) and no electrical refrigeration.
do_not: Smoke food using evergreen wood (pine, cedar)
Consume preserved food showing signs of fuzzy mold or foul odor
Store food caches near sleeping quarters (attracts predators)
sources: USDA Guide to Home Food Preservation
